title: B-tree indexes and page structure
description: Understand how SQL Server physically stores data using 8 KB pages and B-tree index structures.

data.text: Every table and index in SQL Server is stored as a collection of 8 KB pages arranged in a B-tree structure. Understanding this physical layout explains why indexes speed up queries and why bad index design hurts performance.

SQL Server stores data in fixed-size units called pages. Each page is exactly 8 KB. A page contains row data, a slot array, and a small header. When a row is wider than 8 KB, SQL Server moves large columns to Row-Overflow pages and leaves a 24-byte pointer behind.

data.title: View page counts for a table
data.content: Use this query to see how many pages a table or index is using.
data.code:
SELECT
    t.name AS TableName,
    i.name AS IndexName,
    p.page_count,
    p.used_page_count,
    p.data_page_count
FROM sys.dm_db_partition_stats AS p
JOIN sys.tables AS t ON t.object_id = p.object_id
JOIN sys.indexes AS i ON i.object_id = p.object_id
    AND i.index_id = p.index_id
WHERE t.name = 'Orders';

data.text: A B-tree index is a balanced tree with three main parts: the root page at the top, intermediate index pages in the middle, and leaf pages at the bottom. The leaf level holds the actual data for clustered indexes, or index keys plus row locators for nonclustered indexes.

data.title: Key points about B-tree levels
items: Root page: one page only; contains pointers to intermediate pages
Intermediate pages: navigate the tree to the right leaf page
Leaf pages: contain the final key values and either the data row or a row locator

data.caption: Simplified B-tree structure with root, intermediate, and leaf levels
data.definition:
graph TD
    subgraph Root
        R[Root Page]
    end
    subgraph Intermediate
        M1[Intermediate 1]
        M2[Intermediate 2]
    end
    subgraph Leaf
        L1[Leaf 1]
        L2[Leaf 2]
        L3[Leaf 3]
        L4[Leaf 4]
    end
    R --> M1
    R --> M2
    M1 --> L1
    M1 --> L2
    M2 --> L3
    M2 --> L4

data.title: Page density matters
data.text: If pages are full, the tree is shorter and queries are faster. If pages are sparse, the same data needs more pages and more I/O. Fill factor lets you control how full pages are when indexes are rebuilt.

When a row grows beyond the space available on its current page, SQL Server may move the entire row to a new page and leave a forwarding pointer behind. This is called a forwarded record. It is common in tables with varchar(max) columns that change size frequently. Page splits happen when a new row is inserted into a full page and the page is divided into two.

data.title: Check for forwarded records
data.content: Forwarded records force extra I/O during scans. This query shows how many exist on a heap.
data.code:
SELECT
    OBJECT_NAME(ps.object_id) AS table_name,
    ps.forwarded_record_count
FROM sys.dm_db_index_physical_stats(DB_ID(), NULL, NULL, NULL, 'LIMITED') AS ps
WHERE ps.forwarded_record_count > 0;

data.title: Takeaway
points: SQL Server stores everything in 8 KB pages arranged in a B-tree
The B-tree has root, intermediate, and leaf levels
Page splits and forwarded records degrade read performance
Fill factor and index design directly affect page density
data.takeaway: Good index design starts with understanding how pages and B-trees map physical reads to logical results.
